title: Grammars, parse trees and pushdown automata
subtitle: Add one stack to a finite automaton and it can count and match brackets, which is exactly the power of a grammar.

sections.title: Context-free grammars
sections.body:
We just proved that no finite automaton can recognise aⁿbⁿ. So how do we even describe such a language? With a grammar, a set of rewriting rules, like a recipe that keeps expanding one ingredient into a bigger one.

A context-free grammar has variables (S, E…), terminals (a, b, +…), productions A → α, and a start variable. A string is in the language if the start variable can be rewritten into it. The grammar S → aSb | ab generates aⁿbⁿ, the very language no finite automaton can handle. Watch it grow: deriving aaabbb goes S => aSb => aaSbb => aaabbb. Each step rewrites the leftmost variable, and the last frame of the figure adds the parse tree. The two rules wrap an a on the left and a b on the right, again and again, so the counts always match.

questions.prompt: Which language does S → aSb | ab generate?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each use of aSb adds one a on the left and one b on the right.

figures.caption: Figure 3.1.1 — deriving aaabbb
figures.note: Each step rewrites the leftmost variable; the last frame adds the parse tree.

keynotes: A context-free grammar has variables, terminals, productions A → α and a start variable.
A string is in the language if the start variable can be rewritten into it.
S → aSb | ab generates aⁿbⁿ; aaabbb is derived by S => aSb => aaSbb => aaabbb.

sections.title: Parse trees and ambiguity
sections.body:
Sometimes one sentence can be understood in two ways, and you have met it before, like “I saw the man with the telescope.” A grammar can have the same trouble. A parse tree shows which productions built a string, and a grammar is ambiguous if some string has two different parse trees. For a compiler that is a real problem, because the tree is the meaning.

The classic fix is to encode precedence in layers of variables: E → E+T | T, T → T*F | F, F → (E) | a. Now a+a*a has exactly one tree, with * binding tighter than +, so the multiplication is grouped under the addition, as the figure shows. A grammar is ambiguous when some string has more than one parse tree.

choices.text: Some string has more than one parse tree.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Different trees can mean different values.

figures.caption: Figure 3.2.1 — unambiguous expression grammar
figures.note: The tree shows the multiplication grouped under the addition.

sections.title: Simplification and normal forms
sections.body:
Messy grammars are hard to analyse, so before we work with one we tidy up: remove useless variables, ε-productions and unit productions (A → B). Then we can squeeze it into a standard shape. Chomsky normal form allows only A → BC and A → a. Greibach normal form allows only A → aα. Any CFL (without ε) has grammars in both forms. BNF is the notation compilers use for language syntax.

Convert S → aSb | ab to Chomsky normal form. Introduce A → a and B → b, and split the long rule: S → AC | AB, C → SB. Every production now has exactly two variables or one terminal on the right, so the form is regular and easy to use. A production allowed in Chomsky normal form is A → BC or A → a.

worked.why: Convert S → aSb | ab to Chomsky normal form.
Introduce A → a, B → b and split: S → AC | AB, C → SB.
worked.math: S\to AC\mid AB,\ C\to SB,\ A\to a,\ B\to b

questions.prompt: A production allowed in Chomsky normal form is…

choices.text: A → BC (two variables) or A → a (one terminal).

keynotes: Before analysis remove useless variables, ε-productions and unit productions (A → B).
Chomsky normal form allows only A → BC and A → a; Greibach normal form only A → aα.
S → aSb | ab becomes S → AC | AB, C → SB, A → a, B → b in Chomsky normal form.

sections.title: Pushdown automata
sections.body:
Here is the machine that matches a grammar’s power, and you can picture it easily. Take a finite automaton and give it a stack of plates: it can put a plate on top, or take the top one off, but see only the top. That is a PDA, an NFA with a stack.

A move depends on the state, the input symbol (or ε) and the top of the stack, and changes the state and replaces the top with a string. To recognise aⁿbⁿ: push an A for every a, pop one for every b, and accept if the stack returns to its bottom marker Z. Watch the stack on the right of the figure: aaabbb is accepted. But aabbb is rejected, because one b too many makes the stack run dry. The stack lets a PDA count, which a DFA cannot.

questions.prompt: What lets a PDA check aⁿbⁿ but not a DFA?

choices.text: The stack stores an unbounded count of a’s.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Finite states cannot count without bound.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Its memory grows with the input.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: That would be a Turing machine.

figures.caption: Figure 3.4.1 — aaabbb is accepted
figures.note: Top of the stack is the highlighted cell.

figures.caption: Figure 3.4.2 — aabbb is rejected
figures.note: One b too many: the stack runs dry.

problems.prompt: Does the PDA in the figure accept aabbb?
problems.answer: No. After aa, two A’s are pushed; the first two b’s pop them; the third b finds only Z on the stack, so no move is possible: rejected.

sections.title: CFG ⇔ PDA, closure and limits
sections.body:
Grammars generate, PDAs recognise, and the two meet at the same set of languages. Context-free languages are exactly those accepted by PDAs. A grammar becomes a PDA that guesses derivations on its stack, and a PDA becomes a grammar whose variables stand for “go from state p to q popping this symbol”.

Closure here is weaker than for regular languages: CFLs are closed under union, concatenation and star, but not under intersection or complement. And there are limits. The pumping lemma for CFLs (pump two places at once) shows aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not context-free. Can you see why? A single stack can match two counts, but not three. Context-sensitive grammars (α → β with |α| ≤ |β|) sit one level above.

choices.text: No — one stack can match two counts but not three.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The CFL pumping lemma proves it.

keynotes: Context-free languages are exactly those accepted by PDAs.
CFLs are closed under union, concatenation and star, but not under intersection or complement.
The pumping lemma for CFLs pumps two places at once and shows aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not context-free; context-sensitive grammars (|α| ≤ |β|) sit one level above.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
Remember these three, and you can hold the chapter in your head.

  • CFG generates, PDA recognises: same class.
  • Ambiguity lives in the grammar; layering operators removes it.
  • CNF: A → BC | a.
